common_name: Nashville Prickly Pear (Southeastern Clumping Prickly Pear)

planting.note: Detach a pad, let the cut end callous for several days in a dry, shaded spot, then set it upright and partly buried in gritty, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this species is often found rooted into thin soil over limestone outcrops and needs sharp drainage more than fertility.

directions: Root a callused pad section in gritty, sharply drained, limy soil in full sun, choosing a rocky or gravelly bed rather than heavy garden loam. Unlike the sprawling mats of its close relative eastern prickly pear, Nashville prickly pear grows in tighter, more upright clumps of pads and is native to limestone glades, cedar barrens, and rocky open woodlands through the interior Southeast, including Tennessee, Kentucky, Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi. Pale yellow flowers open in late spring atop the pad margins, followed by reddish-purple fruit that ripens by late summer and can be used like other edible pricklypear tunas once the glochids are removed. Its tufted, clump-forming habit makes it a good choice for rock gardens and glade-style plantings where a less sprawling native cactus is wanted.

planting.note: Set a detached, callused joint shallowly in loose, fast-draining sandy soil in full sun; joints of this species detach very easily and root readily wherever they touch bare sand, so handle them with tongs or thick gloves.

directions: Plant a callused joint shallowly in loose, fast-draining sand in full sun and let it sprawl; cockspur prickly pear is a low, mat-forming cactus of coastal dunes, sandhills, and pine flatwoods along the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from the Carolinas through Florida and west into Texas. Its small, easily detached, somewhat cylindrical joints break off at the slightest touch and root wherever they land, an adaptation that lets the plant spread quickly across bare, shifting sand. Pale yellow flowers open in early summer, followed by small reddish fruit, and the dense clusters of fine glochids make this species notorious for hitchhiking on bare feet and shoes along beach trails. It is an excellent, tough choice for stabilizing loose, sandy, full-sun sites where little else will grow.
